text: JSON_VALUE pulls out exactly one scalar value from a JSON string, using a path. The dollar sign is the root of the document, and dots walk down into nested objects -- so a path like dot Vendor dot City reaches straight into a nested object and pulls out that one plain value.

But that only works for a true scalar. Point JSON_VALUE at an array instead, and it comes back NULL -- not an error, just a quiet signal that this path doesn't resolve to a single value. JSON_VALUE was never built to represent a whole array as one scalar.

That's exactly the gap JSON_QUERY fills. Point it at that same array, or at a nested object, and it returns the fragment intact, still as JSON text. Scalar value, use JSON_VALUE. Object or array you need whole, use JSON_QUERY.

Put them together with what you already know from this chapter, and the whole JSON toolkit closes the loop: FOR JSON turns a real query's output into one JSON object, and JSON_VALUE reads individual fields straight back out of it.

That wraps up Chapter 6. You now have the full modern T-SQL toolkit for NULLs, conditionals, safe conversion, and JSON: COALESCE and NULLIF for defaults and guards, IIF and CHOOSE for compact conditionals, TRY_CAST and TRY_CONVERT for safe conversions, STRING_AGG and STRING_SPLIT for joining and splitting text, and FOR JSON, OPENJSON, JSON_VALUE, and JSON_QUERY for moving data in and out of JSON.
Chapter 7 moves into subqueries, CTEs, and views -- building queries out of other queries, starting with single-value subqueries. See you there.
